title: Quiz: ARMv8 Assembly - Fundamentals
prompt: Work through the AArch64 exception levels, the register conventions, integer division by zero, the gdb stepping commands, and what `mov x29, sp` really assembles to.

questions.question: In ARMv8-A, which exception level runs ordinary user applications with the least privilege?
questions.explanation: EL0 runs user applications and has restricted access to instructions, system registers, and memory. EL1 is the operating system kernel, EL2 is a hypervisor, and EL3 is the secure monitor.
questions.hint: User programs run at the lowest numbered exception level.

questions.question: Which block of general-purpose registers is callee-saved, so a function you call must preserve it?
questions.explanation: x19 to x28 are callee-saved, so their values survive a call and a function that wants to use them saves and restores them itself. x0 to x7 pass arguments and return results, x9 to x15 are caller-saved temporaries, and x16 to x18 are the two intra-procedure-call scratch registers and the platform register.
questions.hint: It is the block that ends just before x29, the frame pointer.

questions.question: What happens when a program divides by zero with sdiv or udiv?
options: The instruction raises an exception and the program aborts.
The instruction writes 0 to the destination register.
The instruction sets the Z flag and leaves the destination register unchanged.
The instruction writes the largest representable integer to the destination register.
questions.explanation: AArch64 integer division by zero does not trap. The destination register is set to 0 and execution continues, so the bug surfaces as a wrong result rather than a crash. Neither sdiv nor udiv touches the condition flags.
questions.hint: Nothing traps here, so the question is what value the destination register is left holding.

questions.question: In gdb, how do si and ni differ when the next instruction is a bl to a function?
options: si steps into the called function, while ni runs the whole call and stops on the instruction after it.
si steps over the call, while ni steps into the called function.
si advances one line of source, while ni advances one machine instruction.
si runs until the next breakpoint, while ni executes a single instruction.
questions.explanation: Both commands advance one machine instruction in the ordinary case. On a bl, si steps into the called function, while ni lets the call run to completion and stops at the following instruction.
questions.hint: One of the two steps into a subroutine, the other steps over it.

questions.question: mov x29, sp is an alias. Which instruction does the assembler actually encode?
questions.explanation: When either operand is sp, mov is an alias for the immediate form add xd, xn, 0. The plain register-to-register mov is an alias for orr xd, xzr, xm instead, and that encoding has no way to name sp.
questions.hint: Copying a value is the same arithmetic as adding zero to it.
